<ChapterHeader title="The CLI Manual" />

<Lead>
  `opake` is the reference client. Everything the web app does maps back to a command here, and
  a few things only the CLI does today: shell completions, the background maintenance daemon,
  and the scripting hooks you'd want for pipelines and cron jobs.
</Lead>

## Installing

The CLI is written in Rust. For now it only ships as source; pre-built binaries and a
crates.io release are on the roadmap. Needs Rust 1.75 or later and Git.

<CodeBlock language="sh">git clone https://tangled.org/opake.app/opake</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">cd opake && cargo install --path apps/cli</CodeBlock>

`cargo install` drops the binary at `~/.cargo/bin/opake`. Confirm with `opake --version`.

### Shell completions

Every modern shell gets tab-completion for commands, flags, and subcommands. Pick yours:

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake completions bash > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/opake</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake completions zsh > ~/.zfunc/_opake</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake completions fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/opake.fish</CodeBlock>

---

## How the CLI thinks

Three concepts orient the rest of this page.

**Paths** look like file paths: `report.pdf`, `projects/Q4/notes.md`, `/`. Internally Opake
identifies records by AT-URI (`at://did:plc:xxx/app.opake.document/yyy`), and most commands
accept either — the friendly path when you're at a prompt, the URI when you're piping URIs
around between commands.

**Workspaces** are a separate namespace from your personal cabinet. A bare `opake ls` lists
the cabinet; `opake ls --workspace family-photos` lists that workspace. Every file-touching
command takes the same `--workspace` flag.

**Accounts** stack. `opake account login` adds one; `opake account list` shows the stack;
`--as alice.bsky.social` runs a single command against a specific account without flipping
the default. Useful when you keep a personal account and a work account side by side and
don't want to remember which is currently primary.

Two more globals worth knowing up front: `-v` increases log verbosity (`-vv` debug, `-vvv`
trace), and `--help` works on every subcommand.

---

## 1. Signing in

OAuth through your PDS is the default. The first `opake account login` on a fresh machine also
generates your identity keys and prints a **24-word seed phrase** — write it down before you
close the window. It's the only thing that can bring your identity back if you lose every
device you're signed in on.

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake account login alice.bsky.social</CodeBlock>

If your PDS is somewhere other than the Bluesky cluster, point at it:

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake account login alice.example.com --pds https://pds.example.com</CodeBlock>

For PDSes that don't speak OAuth, fall back to app-password auth:

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake account login alice.example.com --legacy</CodeBlock>

### Coming back to an existing identity

Two ways to sign in on a new machine without generating a fresh identity: pair off an existing
device, or restore from the seed phrase.

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake pair request      # on the new device</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake pair approve      # on the existing device</CodeBlock>

Pairing hands the new device a wrapped copy of your identity keys through your PDS. Both sides
delete their half of the handshake as soon as the transfer is complete.

<SequenceDiagram
  code={pairingCliFlow}
  caption="Device pairing. Both devices coordinate through your PDS; neither side ever transmits your identity keys in the clear."
/>

The other way back in is the seed phrase, in case no paired device is available:

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake recover                    # interactive; prompts for all 24 words</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake recover -f seed-backup.txt</CodeBlock>

### Managing the account stack

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake account list</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake account set-default bob.other.com</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake ls --as alice.bsky.social</CodeBlock>

`--as` accepts a handle or a DID. Handles get resolved fresh on each invocation, so if someone
moved providers recently the CLI still finds them.

---

## 2. Files

`opake upload` puts a file in your cabinet. Destination paths are optional; omit them and the
file lands at the root.

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake upload report.pdf</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake upload report.pdf --dir projects/Q4</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake upload report.pdf --description "Quarterly financial summary"</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake upload report.pdf --workspace team</CodeBlock>

### Reading them back

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake ls</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake ls projects/Q4 -l               # long format, sizes + mime types</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake ls --tag finance</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake tree</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake download report.pdf -o ~/Downloads/</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake cat notes.md                    # decrypts to stdout, pipe-friendly</CodeBlock>

`opake cat` is `opake download --stdout` with a shorter name, and it composes with the rest of
your shell:

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake cat grocery-list.txt | grep -i bread</CodeBlock>

### Moving, renaming, deleting

Rename is a metadata change. Move is structural.

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake metadata rename report.pdf quarterly-report.pdf</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake move report.pdf projects/Q4/</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake mkdir archive</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake rm old-draft.md</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake rm -r archive/</CodeBlock>

### Editing metadata

Document metadata is the part Opake still lets you see in the clear — locally. Names, tags,
and descriptions are encrypted on the wire but rendered in your terminal.

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake metadata show report.pdf</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake metadata describe report.pdf "Q4 financial summary"</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake metadata tag add report.pdf finance</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake metadata tag remove report.pdf draft</CodeBlock>

---

## 3. Sharing

### One file, one person

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake share new secret.pdf bob.bsky.social</CodeBlock>

Opake resolves the handle, fetches Bob's public key from his PDS, wraps the file's content key
against it, and publishes a grant record. Bob sees the file appear in his inbox the next time
his client syncs.

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake share list                      # grants you've issued</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake share inbox                     # grants issued to you</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake share revoke at://did:plc:123/app.opake.grant/tid456</CodeBlock>

Revoking deletes the grant record. It doesn't un-decrypt any copy Bob has already downloaded
— that ship sailed the moment he opened the file. What revocation does buy you is: Bob can't
re-fetch, can't get future updates, and anyone else browsing his repo won't see the grant.

Grab the URI of a specific grant from `opake share list`.

### A group of people

Workspaces are shared folders with a shared encryption key. Adding someone to the workspace
gives them access to every file in it; removing them doesn't re-encrypt history, but it does
cut them off from future changes.

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake workspace create family-photos</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake workspace add-member family-photos alice.bsky.social</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake workspace ls -l</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake upload vacation.jpg --workspace family-photos</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake workspace remove-member family-photos alice.bsky.social</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake workspace leave family-photos</CodeBlock>

---

## 4. Looking someone up

Before you ship a grant to a handle you got over email or Signal, it's sometimes worth
verifying who's on the other end:

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake resolve bob.bsky.social</CodeBlock>

Prints Bob's DID, his PDS, and his X25519 encryption public key. Ask Bob to read his key
fingerprint to you out-of-band; if it matches what `opake resolve` shows, you've confirmed the
identity the grant will actually target.

---

## 5. Background sync

The daemon runs maintenance tasks that don't need to be interactive: the SSE subscription for
live updates, proactive token refresh, and re-encryption passes after a key rotation. You
don't strictly need it for day-to-day use — every interactive command triggers the minimum
sync it needs before running. The daemon just means you don't eat that latency each time.

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake daemon run                      # foreground, for systemd / launchd units</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake daemon list-tasks               # what's queued and what's running</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake daemon install                  # generate + install a launchd or systemd unit</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake daemon uninstall</CodeBlock>

`opake daemon install` picks the right service format for your platform (launchd on macOS,
systemd on Linux) and writes the unit file where the service manager expects it. The service
starts automatically on login.

---

## 6. Starting over

Three escalating levels of clean slate.

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake account logout alice.bsky.social</CodeBlock>

Drops local session credentials for one account. Your encrypted files stay on your PDS
untouched; signing back in picks them right up.

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake rm -r /</CodeBlock>

Empties your cabinet of every document and directory but keeps your identity, keys, and
workspace memberships intact. Good for when you want to repopulate from scratch without
re-pairing or regenerating anything.

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake purge --dry-run</CodeBlock>

<CodeBlock language="sh">opake purge --force</CodeBlock>

The real nuke. Deletes every `app.opake.*` record from your PDS — files, grants, workspaces,
published encryption key, the lot. Your atproto identity itself survives (that belongs to the
PDS, not Opake), but every trace of Opake having been there is gone. `--dry-run` lists what
would go without touching anything.

<Callout type="warning">
  `opake purge --force` is irreversible and doesn't prompt. Grants you've issued to other
  people still point at records that no longer exist after a purge — the links break silently
  on their end.
</Callout>

<Callout type="info">
  Every subcommand takes `--help` for full flags and arguments. Pair it with `-v` when
  something's misbehaving and you want to see the underlying XRPC calls.
</Callout>
